summary: Lists what a standard way of exporting measured IP traffic flow information from routers, measurement probes, and middleboxes needs to do. It is a requirements memo, not a protocol, and fed into the IPFIX working group's later design work.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists what a system for exporting measured IP traffic should support. It describes how packets become flow records and what senders and receivers need from the data transfer.

questions: what is ip flow information export
subtitle: Requirements for measuring IP traffic flows and exporting their records.

tldr.problem: Routers, probes, and middleboxes measure IP traffic, but applications need a defined way to receive and process those measurements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines flow-export roles and requirements for flow classification, metering, record contents, transfer, configuration, and security.
tldr.outcome: This is a requirements memo that fed into IPFIX protocol standardization; it does not specify an export protocol.

today: RFC 3917 is an Informational RFC published in October 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document records requirements for later IPFIX specifications.

sections.title: Flows and the Export Roles
sections.content:
A flow is a set of IP packets seen at an observation point during a time interval. Packets belong to the same flow when they share the configured properties, such as addresses, protocol, or packet treatment. A flow may include all packets at an interface or be as narrow as one packet.

A metering process observes packets and creates flow records. An exporting process sends those records to one or more collecting processes, which receive them. The memo defines these roles but leaves what a collector does with records outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow groups packets according to selected properties. One process measures packets, another sends the resulting records, and a collector receives them.

sections.title: Applications That Use Flow Data
sections.content:
The requirements are derived from five application areas: usage-based accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, attack and intrusion detection, and quality-of-service monitoring. Each needs different measurements, but all need a way to export data from where traffic is observed.

The memo notes that these requirements do not cover every possible use. For example, its flow summaries include first- and last-packet times but do not provide timestamps for every packet, which would be needed for some jitter measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: People use flow records to account for traffic, plan networks, and look for unusual activity. The memo uses these needs to decide what an export system should provide.

sections.title: Classifying and Metering Traffic
sections.content:
A metering process must be configurable to distinguish flows using interface, IP address, protocol, and TCP or UDP port information. It must support full and prefix matches for addresses. When relevant at an observation point, it must also distinguish by MPLS label or DiffServ Code Point.

The process must either meter packets reliably or report when it cannot. It must timestamp the first and last packet with at least one-centisecond resolution, support synchronization with UTC, and detect flow expiration. If sampling or overload behavior changes, affected old records must be ended and kept separate from records produced under the new behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The meter sorts packets using properties that operators can configure. If it misses packets or changes how it measures them, collectors need to be told so records from different conditions are not combined.

sections.title: Exporting Records Safely
sections.content:
Flow records must be able to report key attributes such as source and destination addresses, protocol, ports when applicable, packet and byte counts, first and last timestamps, and identifiers for the observation point and exporting process. The data model must allow flexible records and future attributes.

Transfer must use a congestion-aware protocol and provide confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. A collector must be able to detect record loss. Push reporting is required, while pull reporting is optional. The system must support collection from hundreds of exporting processes.
sections.plainLanguage: A report needs to identify the traffic it describes and how much traffic was measured. It must travel in a way that limits congestion, protects the data, and lets the receiver detect missing records.
